extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and critics writing or judging heroic drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and staging heroic plays modelled on the heroic (epic) poem: use of supernatural/enthusiastic elements, spectacle (battles, drums, trumpets), and a heroic conception of character that permits passion and extraordinary deeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gods, spirits, and magic in heroic poetry/plays
rubrics_metrics.description: An heroic poet (or dramatist) may employ the ministry of gods, the precipitation of the soul, fury of a prophet, spectres, visions, and magic-palaces as part of the poem's fabric; such supernatural elements are part of what makes epic/heroic writing noble and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: the ghost of Polydorus in Virgil, the Enchanted Wood in Tasso, the Bower of Bliss in Spencer. Objections about improbability are answered by noting that many ages and religions believed in magic and apparitions, which is 'foundation enough for poetry.' Poets can explicate doctrines of separated beings more satisfactorily than philosophers because they follow fancy. Anti-pattern: omitting these elements risks removing some of the greatest beauties of heroic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from strict verisimilitude / allowance for visionary objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic poet is not tied to a bare representation of what is true or exceeding probable; he may 'let himself loose to visionary objects' and represent things not dependent on sense or ordinary knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suspension of strict probability gives the poet a freer scope for imagination. It is sufficient that such things may be in nature or believed, rather than strictly demonstrable; therefore improbability alone is not a disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model heroic plays by the rules of the heroic (epic) poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic plays should be modeled on the rules and spirit of the heroic poem — the most noble, pleasant, and instructive way of writing in verse — and thus may borrow epic modes and devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly states he has 'modelled my heroic plays by the rules of an heroic poem' and uses this as justification for his dramatic choices. Implication: adopt epic diction, scope, and devices when composing heroic drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include spectacle (drums, trumpets, representations of battles) to raise imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Warlike instruments (drums, trumpets) and even the presentation of fighting on stage are appropriate and often necessary in an heroic play to raise the imagination and persuade the audience that what they behold is really performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare used such devices; Jonson uses off-stage trumpet and fighting-sounds. These devices help the poet 'endeavour an absolute dominion over the minds of the spectators.' Anti-pattern: avoiding approved stage devices merely because they have been used by mountebanks or low entertainers is unwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama's advantage: represent rather than merely relate
rubrics_metrics.description: One clear advantage of drama over epic poetry is that drama 'represents to view what the poem only does relate,' and thus drama should exploit visual and performed representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenic, physical, and performative elements (sets, action, spectacle) to accomplish what verse-only narration cannot; Horace's maxim cited: things presented to the eyes affect the mind more easily than things presented to the ears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to command the audience's imagination (absolute dominion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should strive for near-total control over the spectators' imaginations during the performance, assisting the audience's fancy rather than leaving all deception to chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers ought to 'help [fancy's] operation' by using stagecraft and poetic devices to make the audience accept and be moved by the representation; successful manipulation of imagination is a central aim of heroic drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow heroes human passions and imperfections (not mere moral exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes in heroic drama need not be rigidly perfect moral exemplars; great authors (Homer, Tasso) portray heroes with pride, impatience, insolence, and other strong passions — qualities that make them interesting and believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Achilles and Rinaldo are praised despite (or because of) their fiery tempers and contempts for kings. The French standard of measuring love and honour 'by drams and scruples' is rejected; heroic characters may display great spirit and occasional breaches of strict moral virtue without forfeiting heroic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit extraordinary or improbable heroic actions if plausibly motivated
rubrics_metrics.description: Daring or seemingly improbable feats (e.g., a stranger appeasing factions, calming armies by personal presence) are acceptable when grounded in character, reputation, circumstance, or historical precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense of Almanzor: his prior gallantry, known personage, and presence of the king's guards make his actions sufficiently plausible; historical analogues (e.g., Caesar's calming of mutinies or single presentations before armies) support acceptance. Anti-pattern: condemning extraordinary actions as 'impossible' without considering motive and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard effective devices because of vulgar or prior misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage methods or devices that have proven effective (even if used by low entertainers) should not be abandoned merely for their prior associations with mountebanks or vulgarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a physician should not forbear an approved medicine because a mountebank has used it with success; similarly, drums, trumpets, or spectacle remain valid even if popular or theatrical troupes used them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer enthusiastic, visionary poetic mode over sober historical narration for heroic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An heroic poem/play should aim at the 'furentis animi vaticinatio' (the frenzy/prophecy of a rapturous spirit) rather than a dry historiographical mode; too close a following of historical truth (as Lucan) can produce a sober, didactic effect rather than true heroic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Lucan: he 'walks soberly afoot, when he might fly.' To achieve the noblest parts of heroic writing, poets should allow enthusiasm, prophecy, and vision to enter the work; anti-pattern: treating heroic poetry as mere history or philosophical instruction.
